title: Rotating Chore Chart
story: Your shared house has a chore chart: a fixed list of chores and one name beside each. Every week the names move down one place, and whoever falls off the bottom wraps to the top.
After a holiday the chart is several weeks behind. You want to move the names down that many places in one go, rewriting the list you have rather than making a new one.
task: Write rotateChores(names, k). Move every name k places towards the end, wrapping around: the name at index i ends up at index (i + k) % names.length.
Change names in place and return nothing. k can be larger than the list, and the list can be empty. Try to use only O(1) extra memory.
constraints: Names are non-empty strings and may repeat.

examples.explanation: Everyone moves down 2 places. Dev and Eli wrap to the top, in the same order.
Moving 3 places brings everyone back, so 7 places is the same as 7 % 3 = 1 place. Caro wraps to the top.

hints: Rotating [A, B, C, D, E] by 2 gives [D, E, A, B, C]. Which block moved to the front, and did the order inside each block change?
Two blocks, [A, B, C] and [D, E], swap places, keeping their inner order. Rotating by the list length changes nothing, so first set k to k % n.
Reverse the whole list: [E, D, C, B, A]. The blocks are in the right places, but each is backwards. What fixes that?
With k = k % n: reverse the whole list, then the first k items, then the remaining n - k. One helper reverses a range in place with two pointers swapping inward.
bruteForce: Rotate by one place, k times, by moving the last name to the front and shifting everyone else down.

Each one-place rotation moves all n names, so this costs n × k steps, and with 100,000 names and k in the billions it never finishes. Reducing k to k % n still leaves up to n² moves. Copying into a new list takes O(n) time but needs a second list of n names.

js: * @param {string[]} names  one name per chore, top to bottom
* @param {number} k  places to move everyone down
py: def rotate_chores(names: list[str], k: int) -> None:

tests.note: empty list with k > 0: watch out for k % 0
same as moving up by one
huge k: one step at a time is far too slow
k larger than the length, not a multiple

js: k = k % n; // full laps change nothing
reverse(names, 0, n - 1); // blocks swap places, but each is backwards
reverse(names, 0, k - 1); // fix the block that wrapped to the top
reverse(names, k, n - 1); // fix the rest
py: k %= n  # full laps change nothing
reverse(names, 0, n - 1)  # blocks swap places, but each is backwards
reverse(names, 0, k - 1)  # fix the block that wrapped to the top
reverse(names, k, n - 1)  # fix the rest
walkthrough: Rotating right by k moves the last k names in front of the others, each block keeping its order. Reversing the whole list puts both blocks in place but flips each one. Reversing each block flips it back.
• Reversing the whole list gives [Eli, Dev, Caro, Ben, Ana]. Dev and Eli are now at the top, but in backwards order.
• Reversing the first 2 names gives [Dev, Eli, Caro, Ben, Ana].
• Reversing the last 3 names gives [Dev, Eli, Ana, Ben, Caro], which is the final result.
• Reduce k first, but check for an empty list before that, because k % 0 gives NaN in JavaScript and raises an error in Python.

• "In place" means changing the list you were given. names = newList only repoints your local variable. In Python, names[:] = names[-k:] + names[:-k] does write into the original, but builds a full copy first.
solution.timeWhy: Three reversals, and each name is swapped at most twice.
solution.spaceWhy: Swaps happen inside the list; only a few index variables are used.
solution.takeaway: Swapping two blocks of an array in place is "reverse the whole thing, then reverse each block". Two-pointer reversal solves many in-place rearrangement problems.
